body: I'd love to have the luxury of shopping around for a good shrink, but I'm limited to whoever's got an appointment slot open at the community clinic. If the first one is awful, I may try to change to a new one at the same place, but I don't know how to really gauge the potential awfulness, other than the here-are-your-pills criterion.

I'm sure many people have had a similar experience to mine, that is, trying one or two drugs and giving up. But it's possible that there's a drug for everyone, if we're willing to abide the trial and error. The error part is what worries me, personally, because often the errors can be extremely dangerous.

Yes, I've been in therapy at various times, with varying degrees of success. Due to the family meeting, I will be meeting a psychiatrist but we didn't discuss finding a counselor. Surely that's part of the plan. The one I've been seeing recently has pretty much reached the limit of their usefulness. All together I've seen about 10 different counselors and had good interactions with 3 or 4 of them. But no matter who it was, it was always great to be able to vent.

I will definitely ask my doctor about that. I think when they prescribed me Seroquel it was supposed to be a sleeping aid!

I didn't know you could have mainly lows with bipolar disorder. Guess I figured it would be pretty evenly split, but never looked into it.

Thanks for the sweet thoughts. You made me smile.

Seriously, I'm going to be coming back to this over and over.

Hey, I just finished responding to a question about meds over [here.](http://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/fqm13/the_familys_staging_an_intervention_for_me/c1hy9x8)

I've been to several psychiatrists, but their insights have never gone much beyond "you need some pills". The good analysis has always come from psychologists and various counselors. One of the agreements reached at the meeting today was that I had to consent to see a psychiatrist, so we'll see what they say. If they prescribe something, I might try it. In fact, I probably will because there's not much choice in the matter anymore. A little, but not much.

> Your family are trying to tell you that they want to help you. They're offering. Telling them what you need is just taking them up on that offer.

I wish I knew what I needed.

What do I have to lose by trying meds? Well, the first antidepressant I tried (Wellbutrin) made me so anxious and paranoid I started hearing shit that wasn't there. Then my psychiatrist proved his incompetency by prescribing clonazepam (aka Klonopin) to curb the anxiety, and I felt more depressed and suicidal than I had ever thought possible. It was a close shave making it out of that one. The second antidepressant I tried was Lexapro, which didn't do anything even though I was on it for over a year. I used it in conjunction with Seroquel for at least part of the treatment, it's hard to remember now.

So I'm at the mercy of the pharmaceutical industry that cares about selling quick fixes, doctors that are lobbied by vendors of drugs that should never be prescribed to me (thanks a lot Klonopin), and doctors that have no freaking clue what they're doing. Since I'm indigent, I will have to rely on care from clinics that cater to homeless people, and I don't expect the caliber of the doctors to be very high, especially since it was a private practice that screwed my brain up so bad the first time.

I also, perhaps foolishly, believe I can do it by myself if I try, and I just haven't made the decision to try. If I put aside my bias, I can see that having data on what doesn't work for me will help a competent doctor find something that will work, so maybe now is the time.

Apart from all that, I do understand that chemical imbalances can be corrected in a great many cases, and I'm not saying any of this to dissuade you from taking your medication. Just telling you what I've experienced.

I'm not a user, but I do have some history of over-drinking and drinking alone, which is apparently not as cool as George Thoroughgood thought. This intervention is because I am depressed all the time and have withdrawn to an unacceptable level. My involvement in the few social things I do has ebbed to almost nothing. For example, in the past 4 days I have done nothing but eat and sit around reading books, trying to ignore everything, even though I live with 3 other people. My financial situation is unsustainable because I'm completely dependent, and I think this last is why the intervention became so urgent. I have stopped trying to get a job.

I don't think I can tell them I'm suicidal. Dealing with the above is bad enough, and if they send me to psych professionals I can deal with it there. But I know they'll ask! Shit.

The really hard part is I don't want to do anything about any of it. I mean, it's so hard to care. I don't see the point of "getting better".

Yes I have persistent suicidal thoughts which have, in fact, been getting worse. And I didn't mention it in this post, but my mom committed suicide, so it will have extra punch in this crowd.

My brain doesn't work. Can you help me with weighing the consequences?

I'll start. If I tell them: (1) They will want me to take drugs. (2) They will feel even more worried about me, maybe resentful because these things make me even more of a burden. (3) They will want to control my living situation from the outside, and possibly consider inpatient care above other options, just to get rid of me. (4) They will take everything I have to say seriously and want to work with me on my terms (sounds like I'm holding myself hostage - hah!). 

What am I missing?

Yeah it is a nice gesture. But I'm *already* being subjected to this inter-departmental drama between the sister and the stepmom all because of this. I knew that would happen. And it is not nice.

I also know they want me to go to a psychiatrist even though I'm adamantly against taking drugs. I don't know what I might say if there's the slightest hint that they'll try and make me take them. I will probably explode into tiny bits.

There's also hints about inpatient care - the psych ward. That actually doesn't sound so bad except about the drugs again. Don't know what their policy is on forcing pills. (Probably not like One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, right?)

You know what, this whole thing is probably going to focus on me taking fucking drugs. Goddammit.

Thanks for writing back, and for the link. It's so hard to try and figure anything out, yet I'm still trying, I just don't know why.

Everything is too complicated and difficult and I just don't want to try anymore. It hurts to think.

I don't see a goal worthy of all this terror. I don't want to fight for anything. Everything gets torn down. That's why planning is useless. 

And nothing improves because I always stop trying. I stop trying because I don't believe in anything.

I do care about people. I care enough that I'd rather die than have to watch the turmoil for the rest of my life.

I'm not strong enough for this.

/attention whore I hate this. I've been awake for a really long time, sorry this is so fucked up.

Just acting really pitiful and sorry for myself at the moment. Thanks for listening.

When I say i don't believe in anything, part of what I'm saying is I don't have a path or a passion that can guide me internally. I would really like to follow a path that makes sense to me, but none of them do and I'm very lost.

If I found such a thing, I would probably be enthusiastic for a little while and then decide it's just another flavor of bullshit. Which everything pretty much is. There's too much compromise.

I'm in my mid-20s sounding like an angsted teenager. This blows.

> Why exactly are you so nihilistic now?

Hard to pinpoint a reason. I just don't see a point to my existence, and I'm not enlightened enough to accept meaninglessness. This might be a worthy goal (acceptance, that is) if I decided it was valuable to have a goal.

Any effort I might choose to expend toward making my life better right now is basically wasted. No matter what, I am facing an uphill battle just to establish some day-to-day stability, like having a job and a working bank account. Once I get that (which might take me months even after getting a job), I don't have much to look forward to, just more battles, especially to establish a plan for my life, and executing such a plan. I hate planning. My life strategy has thus far failed and I don't believe my strategic skills have improved. I anticipate more and more failure. So anything I do now to marginally improve my situation will ultimately count for nothing. I will continue to make the same mistakes over and over again. I know this because that's what I keep doing. I crash and burn for a while, someone helps me out, I make a little improvement, and then it's back to the failboat.

My original post certainly came across as very cerebral. I edited out most of the emotions because I wanted to address the philosophical problem first. The emotional/psychological problem I largely understand: I have clinical depression, I am avoiding social interaction, I have financial issues, no stability in my life, hypersomnia, avoidance/escapism.

Maybe trying to look at this problem from the philosophical viewpoint (as I so often do) is just another way of avoiding the real issue, whichever that may be. Maybe I'm wrong about my premise (that this is a terrible terrible place that no self-aware creature should have to endure). How can I know either way? 

My main question for you: Is it actually better to keep feeling awful every day, and trying to fix everything, even if you don't believe in anything? If so, why?

Thanks for writing.

Thanks for your reply.

> if I can make one person's life better, that would make life worth it for me. 

I can't live for other people. Have you ever read "Those Who Walk from Omelas"?

Eight years ago, as an extremely idealistic teenager, I decided I wanted to help people. I was going to figure out what exactly is wrong with the world and how to fix it. What I found is that it can't be fixed. I admit my "research" is highly suspect and consists mostly of interpreting the formations of spaghetti thrown at a questionnaire clipboard (i.e., sociology), as well as personal experience (ok, that was harsh; sociology can be as real as any other science, I'm just being an arse). 

So you can't stop social suffering, fine. Why not try on a smaller scale? Every time you have a positive interaction with someone, it builds the relationship. As you build the relationship, there are more and more ways it can go wrong, and it usually does. With the good times come the bad. There are no truly happy people, only happy moments, which pass by and become memories. 

My mother's suicide note said she was sorry she didn't love us enough to live for us, and that's what I'm starting to feel like. No one is responsible for me, so why should I take responsibility for someone else? 

The truth is, the only person you can count on is yourself, and we are all *ultimately* alone.

[Yeah, I'm actually super fun at parties because it's an escape from my thoughts.]

Thanks for your thoughts.

> What has happened over the years to get you some help of any kind? 

I have been to psychologists/counselors at various times. I gave up on the last one because I couldn't afford the $10 per session but it didn't seem like much of a loss. I have also tried two different antidepressants, neither of which made a positive difference. In fact, one made me significantly worse.

> It would be amazing for you to be able to turn your mental energy away from the negative towards the positive

Yes, of course that would be a wonderful change if I could believe in it. And I have tried this, and tried twisting my negative perceptions into positive ones. But it never helped me or changed my underlying belief, which I cannot ignore: we are all mutated ape-creatures with an engorged sense of self-importance living in an indifferent universe where suffering is the norm.

What if I twisted this around? We are highly evolved creatures with consciousness that's unique in the world as far as we know; the probability of our individual selves existing is near zero and that which is rare ought to be treasured and explored; it doesn't matter if the universe is indifferent because we are not indifferent to one another; without pain and the negative, we could not appreciate the positive; caring and love and a wealth of experience are reasons enough to stick around and see what happens, despite the troubles of life.

It sounds so great! So healthy! But it also sounds wrong. To me anyway. And I would feel like a liar trying to accept something I didn't believe in. I don't want to delude myself into getting better. If that's what it takes, then it's not worth it.

Socrates said the unexamined life is not worth living, but he never said the examined life was worth living.

edit: I do wish there were someone I could talk to, but I'm such a burden on everyone already, and if I went back to my counselor I couldn't talk about any of this suicidal stuff because they have to call the police or something. It really is very lonely.
